title: Great Explorers · Episode 3
chapters: Scurvy: the cure that kept getting lost
Lewis and Clark: across a continent

units.t: Great Explorers. Episode three.
In this episode: James Cook's voyages, Scurvy: the cure that kept getting lost and Lewis and Clark: across a continent.
Part one. James Cook's voyages.
A farm labourer's son became the Pacific's greatest mapmaker.
His voyages changed science, and the fate of the peoples he met.
Labourer to captain.
James Cook was born in Yorkshire in 1728, the son of a farm labourer.
He learned seamanship on coal ships out of Whitby, joined the Royal Navy in 1755 and rose quickly.
During the Seven Years' War he helped chart the St Lawrence River, then made his name mapping Newfoundland with remarkable precision.
Largely self-taught, he was a skilled mathematician and astronomer, rare for someone without a privileged education.
In 1768 he was chosen to command a scientific voyage to the Pacific aboard the Endeavour, a converted Whitby coal ship.
Venus and the south.
The official purpose of the first voyage, 1768 to 1771, was to watch Venus cross the Sun from Tahiti on 3 June 1769.
Transits come in pairs about eight years apart, with over a century between pairs, and astronomers hoped to calculate the Earth-Sun distance.
Cook also carried secret orders to seek the great southern continent, Terra Australis.
Aboard was the wealthy young botanist Joseph Banks, who collected thousands of plants with Daniel Solander.
Cook mapped both islands of New Zealand, partly seen by Abel Tasman in 1642.
Early encounters with Māori ended in bloodshed.
In April 1770 he reached Australia's east coast at Kamay, Botany Bay, named for Banks's new plants, where Gweagal men opposed the landing.
On Possession Island in August 1770, Cook claimed the east coast for Britain without its peoples' consent.
Reef and science.
In June 1770 the Endeavour ran aground on the Great Barrier Reef.
The crew threw cannons, ballast and supplies overboard and, once afloat, slowed the leak by drawing a sail packed with oakum and wool under the hull: fothering.
They limped to the Endeavour River, near Cooktown, where repairs took about seven weeks.
There they had extended contact with the Guugu Yimithirr people and recorded the word 'kangaroo', from gangurru.
Banks and Solander brought back many plants new to European science, and artist Sydney Parkinson made hundreds of drawings before dying on the voyage home.
The first voyage was still deadly: over a third of the crew died, mostly of disease caught at Batavia, Jakarta.
Cook later fought scurvy with fresh food, sauerkraut and strict cleanliness, and lost very few men to it.
The later voyages.
On the second voyage, 1772 to 1775, Cook carried a copy of John Harrison's marine chronometer, accurate enough to calculate longitude at sea, and praised it.
He crossed the Antarctic Circle, showing any southern continent must lie in the icy far south, not the temperate latitudes Europeans imagined.
On the third voyage, 1776 to 1780, searching for a Northwest Passage above North America, he became the first European known to reach Hawai'i, in 1778.
He sailed north through the Bering Strait until ice blocked the way.
Back in Hawai'i, amid rising tensions over a stolen boat, he was killed in a confrontation at Kealakekua Bay on 14 February 1779.
His crew completed the voyage without him.
A contested legacy.
Cook's charts and Banks's enthusiasm for Botany Bay influenced Britain's decision to send convicts to New South Wales.

The First Fleet arrived in January 1788, but Captain Arthur Phillip found Botany Bay unsuitable, with poor soil and little fresh water, and moved about 12 kilometres north to Sydney Cove in Port Jackson, a harbour Cook had noted but not entered.
The founding, on 26 January, is now Australia Day, which many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people mourn as the beginning of invasion.
Cook's maps were so accurate that some were used for over a century, and his voyages advanced botany, astronomy and knowledge of the Pacific.
Yet for many Aboriginal Australians, Māori and Pacific peoples, his arrival marks dispossession and disease.
Both views reflect real history, and holding both is part of understanding the past honestly.
The key idea: James Cook, a farm labourer's son, taught himself navigation, astronomy and surveying and became a brilliant chart maker.
Part two. Scurvy: the cure that kept getting lost.
For centuries a disease killed more sailors than storms and battles.
The cure was found, forgotten and found again, and the final answer turned on a lucky choice of guinea pig.
The sailor's plague.
After a couple of months on salted meat and ship's biscuit, sailors grew exhausted.
Their gums swelled and bled, teeth loosened, bruises appeared from nowhere and old wounds reopened.
Even long-healed fractures could come apart.
Untreated, scurvy killed.
On George Anson's voyage around the world in the 1740s, about 1,900 men set out and only a few hundred returned, with disease, mostly scurvy, killing far more than enemy action.
Vasco da Gama also lost many men to it.
The cause is a lack of vitamin C, which helps build collagen, the protein that holds skin, vessels, gums and scars together.
Without it, tiny vessels leak and wounds cannot knit.
Humans, other apes, guinea pigs and some bats and birds cannot make vitamin C, so we must eat it.
Lind's experiment.
In 1747 the naval surgeon James Lind chose twelve sailors with scurvy and split them into six pairs.
On the same basic diet, each pair received a different remedy: cider, dilute sulphuric acid, vinegar, seawater, a spice and garlic paste, or two oranges and a lemon daily.
The citrus pair improved dramatically, one being fit for duty within about a week.
Comparing treatments side by side in similar patients makes this a landmark of medicine.
Yet Lind treated citrus as one remedy among many.
He also boiled juice into a concentrate, and vitamin C breaks down with heat, so it was far weaker than fresh fruit.
Nobody knew why citrus worked, and James Cook credited several remedies, including sauerkraut.
His fresh food from ashore probably mattered more.
Lemons, then limes.
Urged on by the physician Gilbert Blane and others, the Royal Navy began issuing lemon juice to all sailors in 1795, usually in the daily grog.
Scurvy largely vanished from the fleet.
Then the cure was quietly undermined.
In the mid nineteenth century the navy switched to cheaper limes from the West Indies.
Limes contain considerably less vitamin C than lemons, and processing the juice could destroy more.
British sailors earned the nickname limeys, but on long Arctic expeditions in the 1870s scurvy struck men who had taken their lime juice.
Many experts wrongly concluded that citrus did not work.
Others blamed bacteria or poisons in tinned meat.
A lucky guinea pig.
The breakthrough came in 1907.
The Norwegian scientists Axel Holst and Theodor Frølich were studying beriberi and fed guinea pigs a grain-only diet.
Instead the animals developed scurvy.
It was luck: rats and mice make their own vitamin C and would have shown nothing.
Now scurvy could be studied in the lab and foods could be tested for their power to prevent it.
In the late 1920s Albert Szent-Györgyi isolated a compound that, in the early 1930s, he showed prevented scurvy.
It was renamed ascorbic acid, meaning "against scurvy".
Norman Haworth worked out its structure and helped synthesise it, and in 1937 Szent-Györgyi and Haworth won Nobel Prizes.
Scurvy today.
With vitamin C cheap and plentiful in fruit and vegetables, scurvy is rare in wealthy countries, but it has not disappeared.

Doctors still see it in people with severely limited diets, such as some older people living alone, people with alcohol dependence or certain eating disorders, and occasionally children with very selective eating.
Because it is now unusual, it can be missed: bleeding gums and bruising have many causes.
Treatment with vitamin C, guided by a doctor, usually brings rapid improvement.
The story carries a lasting lesson.
Lind found strong evidence in 1747, yet confusion, cost-cutting and wrong theories meant sailors kept dying for generations.
A cure is only as good as our understanding of why it works.
The key idea: Scurvy, caused by a lack of vitamin C, killed huge numbers of sailors by weakening the collagen that holds the body together.
Part three. Lewis and Clark: across a continent.
In 1804 a small army party set out to cross North America to the Pacific and back.
They found no easy river route, but they mapped a continent and depended on the people who already lived there.
Jefferson's big question.
In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France for about fifteen million dollars, roughly doubling the young country.
President Jefferson wanted to know what the land held, from plants and rivers to the Native nations living there.
Above all he hoped for a practical water route linking the Missouri to the Pacific.
He chose his secretary, army captain Meriwether Lewis, to lead.
Lewis asked his former army comrade William Clark to share command, and the two worked as genuine equals.
Lewis spent months studying botany, astronomy and medicine and buying supplies, including gifts for Native leaders.
The Corps of Discovery, thirty to forty soldiers and boatmen, with York, an enslaved man owned by Clark, and Lewis's dog Seaman, left near St Louis in May 1804.
Winter, and Sacagawea.
By late 1804 the Corps had travelled over two thousand kilometres up the Missouri to the Mandan and Hidatsa villages in what is now North Dakota, and built a fort to survive the winter.
Only one member died on the whole journey, Sergeant Charles Floyd.
There they hired the trader Toussaint Charbonneau, whose wife Sacagawea was a young Shoshone woman captured by Hidatsa raiders as a girl.
Her baby son travelled with them.
Sacagawea is often pictured as the guide, but she was not hired as one and did not know most of the route.
Her value lay elsewhere: she spoke Shoshone, recognised landmarks near her home, and her presence signalled peaceful intent, since war parties did not travel with women.
In August 1805 the Shoshone chief Cameahwait proved to be her brother, which helped secure horses.
No easy passage.
The first great obstacle was the Great Falls of the Missouri, where it took about a month to carry boats and supplies around a series of waterfalls.
Then came the Rockies.
Jefferson had hoped for a short portage between rivers, but the mountains were range after range.
In September 1805 the Corps crossed the Bitterroot Mountains on a steep trail in early snow, with little game.
They were reduced to eating candles and some of their horses.
Starving and sick, they came down into the lands of the Nez Perce, who fed them and helped them build canoes.
They paddled down the Snake and Columbia rivers and in November 1805 reached the Pacific.
The crossing ended the dream of an easy water route.
A vote on the coast.
The Corps had to decide where to spend the winter, and the captains put the question to the whole party.
York's view and Sacagawea's were recorded alongside the soldiers', an extraordinary moment for an enslaved man and a Native woman in that era, though it changed nothing about their status afterwards.
They built Fort Clatsop, near today's Astoria in Oregon, and endured a wet, miserable winter, with rain on most days.
In March 1806 they started for home.
The return journey included a deadly clash with Blackfeet warriors, the only fight of the journey in which people were killed.
What the journey left.
The Corps reached St Louis in September 1806, after more than two years away, to a public that had largely given them up for dead.
Their journals and Clark's maps transformed knowledge of the west, and they described well over a hundred animals and plants new to science, including the grizzly bear and prairie dog.
But the expedition also opened the way for fur traders, settlers and the US government, and over the following century Native nations along the route lost much of their land and many lives.
The travellers' fates were mixed.
Lewis died of gunshot wounds in 1809, widely believed to be suicide.
Clark did not free York for around a decade.
Sacagawea is thought to have died young, around 1812, though some Shoshone traditions say she lived into old age.
The key idea: After the Louisiana Purchase, President Jefferson sent Lewis and Clark to explore the west and find a water route to the Pacific.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What does Cook's early career show?
Answer. Skill and study took a labourer's son to command.
Question two. Why does a lack of vitamin C cause bleeding gums and slow-healing wounds?
Answer. Collagen forms poorly, so tissues and vessels break down.
Question three. What did Jefferson most hope the expedition would find?
Answer. A water route linking the Missouri River to the Pacific.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
